transcript.content: Hi, it's good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, I came in because... honestly, my wife and my director at work kind of forced the issue. I just can’t seem to stop launching projects lately. Like, massive work restructuring plans, scheduling myself for all these new IT certifications, completely tearing out and upgrading my home network... 

Actually, the home network thing was incredibly frustrating because I specifically ordered shielded Cat6a cable, but the vendor sent standard Cat5e. And, you know, if you're going to rip open the drywall to wire a house, you have to future-proof it. You don't want to be stuck with basic gigabit speeds when multi-gig is already the standard for most enterprise access points. I spent like three hours arguing with the distributor on the phone on Tuesday, and they still didn't understand why it mattered. 

But, um... what was I saying? Right, the projects. I just keep starting things, even messaging all these old contacts from my undergrad days to get them in on things. It just gets so intense that I completely blow past normal limits, and I don't even realize I'm doing it until my wife or my boss has to step in and pull the plug.
During these periods, have you been feeling unusually high or irritable?

Yeah, both, I think. Some weeks I feel almost electric... just completely unstoppable, like my brain is compiling everything instantly. But then, if there's even a tiny delay, or if my wife just asks a simple question, I absolutely snap. It feels like everyone is trying to slow me down on purpose. 

Like, the other day, she asked me why I was reorganizing the kitchen pantry by expiration date and barcode type. Which, honestly, makes perfect sense if you understand basic inventory management. We throw away so much food because it gets pushed to the back of the shelves. If we just implemented a simple FIFO system—first in, first out, exactly how we handle server hardware rotations at work—we'd save hundreds of dollars a year. I actually started looking into handheld barcode scanners, specifically the ones with Bluetooth 5.0 so it syncs directly to a local database I was building on my Raspberry Pi. The Pi is great for small home projects, but the I/O bottleneck on a standard micro SD card is a total nightmare if you're trying to run a full SQL database, so I was trying to figure out how to boot the whole OS from an external SSD instead because the read/write speeds are just... 

Wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, irritable. Yeah, I get really irritated when people interrupt my workflow.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day?

Yeah, definitely. It's like a complete system crash. There are these long stretches, definitely more than two weeks, where I wake up feeling like a failed version of myself. Just heavy and flat. Even answering my wife's normal questions feels like too much effort. 

It's strange because, you know, when a server goes down, you can usually check the error logs and figure out what caused the kernel panic. Like, was it a memory leak? A corrupted registry? You just run a diagnostic, isolate the faulty sector, and patch it. I actually wrote a custom script at my last job that would automatically ping the server every 30 seconds, and if it didn't get a response, it would trigger an automated reboot sequence and text my phone. It saved us so much downtime during the Q3 rollout. The only problem was our telecom provider had this weird latency issue with their SMS gateway, so sometimes the text would arrive like four hours after the server was already back up and running, which totally defeats the purpose of real-time alerts. I spent weeks trying to get their Tier 2 support to admit the routing issue was on their end, but they kept blaming our firewall configurations. 

Anyway... yeah, I just feel totally empty and depressed during those times. Like I can't even get out of bed.
What is the longest these high-energy or irritable periods have lasted without stopping?

I don't know, honestly. I've never really timed them. It feels like they just go on until I finally crash. But timing things is actually incredibly difficult if you don't have a standardized metric. Like, we had this massive issue at work a few months ago where the timestamps on our main database servers were drifting. Just by a few milliseconds a day, but over a month, it completely desynced the transaction logs. We were using the default NTP servers, which you'd think would be fine, but the stratum level was too high, so the polling intervals were all over the place. I had to go in and manually configure a local stratum 1 time server using a GPS receiver just to keep everything perfectly synchronized. It was a huge pain, especially because the building's roof access was locked and the facilities manager was on vacation, so I had to mount the antenna near a window and hope the signal-to-noise ratio was decent enough to lock onto the satellites. 

But, uh, anyway... I'm not sure exactly how long the high-energy periods last. It's hard to track.
Has there ever been a time when that unusually high or irritable energy lasted for 7 days in a row or longer?

Seven days... I mean, probably? I really couldn't tell you if it was exactly a week straight. Keeping track of a full seven days is tricky unless you're operating on a strict sprint schedule. Like, at work, we shifted to this Agile framework last year, so everything is broken down into these rigid two-week sprints. Which is supposed to increase efficiency, right? But our Scrum Master insists on doing these daily stand-up meetings that end up taking forty-five minutes because the backend developers keep arguing with the frontend team about API endpoints. 

It's ridiculous. I told them we should just use GraphQL so the client-side can request exactly what it needs and we don't have to keep versioning the REST API every time marketing wants a new data field on the dashboard. But nobody listens to me, they just keep creating more Jira tickets and bloating the backlog. It's like, why even have sprints if you're just going to roll over half the story points to the next week anyway? It completely invalidates the velocity metrics we're supposed to be tracking for the quarterly review, and then upper management gets on my case about resource allocation when the real issue is just terrible project management... 

Wait, sorry. What were we talking about? Oh, seven days. Yeah, I'm really not sure if the energy lasted exactly seven days in a row. I don't really measure it like that.
During those high-energy periods, have you ever heard or seen things that other people said were not there?

Yeah... when I get into those really driven stretches, you know, where I'm barely sleeping and just pushing out these massive deployment plans... I actually did start noticing things. Like, I would hear actual comments coming from the server noise. 

Server rooms are incredibly loud, by the way, mostly because of the HVAC systems. We had this one CRAC unit—Computer Room Air Conditioning—that was constantly vibrating because the fan belt was misaligned. I told the facilities guy to check the tension, but he just sprayed WD-40 on the bearings, which doesn't fix a loose belt, it just masks the squeak for like a day. If you don't maintain the proper airflow, you get hot spots in the racks, and then the thermal sensors automatically throttle the CPUs to prevent a meltdown, which completely tanks the network throughput. I ended up having to buy my own digital anemometer off Amazon just to prove to management that the CFM output was dropping on the cold aisle... 

But anyway, yeah, in that loud humming noise from the racks, I would hear these voices, like comments being spoken directly to me. And I was also reading these hidden threats into my work messages. Like, I'd get a routine Slack update from the dev team, but I could read between the lines and see the actual threats hidden in the syntax of their messages. It was all perfectly clear to me at the time. But, um... yeah, I guess other people didn't hear or see any of that.
Did those voices and hidden threats happen only when you were in those high-energy periods?

No, actually... it wasn't just when I was wired. There have been these long stretches, like a few weeks at a time, where I felt completely flat. Just... normal, I guess? Not super energetic, not depressed either. Just calm. But even during those times, I still heard the voices sometimes, just brief comments. And I still knew that the statuses on Microsoft Teams were coded warnings. 

People think Teams is just a communication tool, but the backend architecture is actually a nightmare if you look at how it handles presence data. It uses this federated signaling protocol, which means your status isn't just updating locally, it's broadcasting across the entire tenant, sometimes even cross-tenant if external access is enabled. And the latency can be horrendous. I've seen people show as "In a meeting" for twenty minutes after the call ended because the presence service in Azure got bottlenecked. I tried explaining this to HR when they tried to write up one of my engineers for being "Away" too much. I had to pull the audit logs from the compliance center just to prove that the polling interval was dropping packets... 

But, uh, yeah. Even when I wasn't in one of those high-energy phases, I still heard the comments and saw the warnings in the statuses.
Was there ever a period of at least two weeks when you were hearing the voices or noticing those hidden warnings while your mood was otherwise normal—not high, irritable, or depressed?

Yeah, definitely. There were definitely times like that. Like I said, there have been these stretches—sometimes lasting a few weeks at a time—where I felt totally calm. Not up, not down, just... flat. But even then, I was still hearing those brief comments when no one was around, and I still fully believed the Teams statuses were coded warnings. 

It's actually fascinating how people use those custom status messages. You know you can set a duration for them now? Like, you can have a message clear after an hour, or at the end of the day. But most people just leave them up forever. We had this one guy in QA who had "Heads down testing" as his status for literally eight months. I mean, at that point, it's not a status, it's a lifestyle. And it completely breaks the utility of the feature. If everyone is always "Heads down," then nobody is, right? It's like when everyone marks their emails as "High Importance." It just creates alert fatigue. I actually wrote a PowerShell script to automatically clear custom statuses across our tenant every Friday at 5 PM just to force people to reset them on Monday, but then the VP of Engineering got mad because he used his status to store links to his current project dashboards... which is a terrible way to manage bookmarks, by the way. You should be using a centralized wiki or at least a pinned tab in the channel. 

But, um... sorry. What did you ask? Oh, right, the two weeks thing. Yeah, there were definitely periods of a few weeks where my mood was totally normal, but I was still getting the warnings and hearing the comments.
